name: AI for School and Educational Leaders 3: AI for Lesson Planning
objectives: Given a standard copied from the official source, write an "I can" objective and three success criteria with AI's help, edited until ready for the board, before asking for activities
Given your objective, write a reusable prompt that gets a full lesson draft from AI, including class length, prior knowledge, materials and sections, with at least two follow-ups
Given an AI lesson draft, check it with the five-point quality checklist and record your changes, fixing every problem found

Given a lesson and a class described by need, plan supports for three groups: needs more support, on level and ready for more, with IEP and 504 accommodations confirmed with a special education colleague
Given the unit your lesson belongs to, draft a unit outline with AI and adjust its pacing, adding a review day and three misconceptions to plan for
For your team or PLC, turn your planning prompts and checklist into a team template and coach others to use it, tracking time saved and quality issues

chapters.name: Chapter 1: Planning a lesson with AI

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Start with the objective, not the activity
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a clear objective and success criteria before asking AI for activities.
This lesson builds toward: Given a standard copied from the official source, you will write an "I can" objective and three success criteria with AI's help, edited until ready for the board, before asking for activities.
AI will happily produce a fun activity that teaches nothing in particular. Backward design prevents that: first decide what students should know or be able to do, then how you will see it, then the activities.
You choose the standard. Copy its exact wording from your state's official standards site or your district's curriculum, not from the AI, because AI can misquote or invent standards codes. Then ask AI to help you turn it into a student-friendly objective ("I can...") and two or three success criteria.
Example prompt: "Here is a standard: [paste it]. Write a one-lesson objective for 6th graders in student-friendly words, and three success criteria that show the objective was met." Edit until you would put it on the board.
Step by step:
- Choose the standard from your state or district source.
- Paste its exact wording into the prompt.
- Ask for an "I can" objective and success criteria.
- Edit until it is clear to students.
- Only then plan activities.
Words to know:
- Backward design: planning from the learning goal, to the evidence, to the activities.
- Success criteria: what students will be able to show when they have met the objective.
- Standard: the official statement of what students should learn, set by your state or district.
Try it now: Pick a standard for a lesson coming up. Copy it from the official source, then use AI to write an "I can" objective and three success criteria. Edit them until they are ready for the board.
You can now start an AI-assisted lesson plan from a real standard, objective and success criteria.

options: The grades students got last year
What students will show when they meet the objective
The list of materials
The teacher's goals for the year
check.why: Success criteria describe the evidence of learning for the objective.

check.q: AI gives you a standard code for your objective. What would you do?
options: Use it, since AI knows the standards
Ask the AI to double-check it
Copy the standard from your state's or district's official source instead
Leave the standard out
check.why: AI can misquote or invent standards, so they come from the official source.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Prompting for the full lesson
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Get a structured lesson plan draft from AI with a reusable prompt.
This lesson builds toward: Given your objective, you will write a reusable prompt that gets a full lesson draft from AI, including class length, prior knowledge, materials and sections, with at least two follow-ups.
With the objective set, ask for the whole lesson in your school's format. A strong prompt gives: grade and subject, class length, the objective and success criteria, what students already know, materials you have, and the sections you want.
Example: "Plan a 50-minute 6th-grade lesson. Objective: [paste]. Success criteria: [paste]. Students already know [x]. Materials: whiteboards, a projector, no devices. Sections: hook (5 min), mini-lesson (10), guided practice (15), independent practice (15), exit ticket (5). Use a table with time, teacher actions, student actions."
Treat the result as a draft from a fast but new colleague. Ask follow-ups: "make the hook connect to students' lives", "add two checks for understanding during the mini-lesson", "shorten guided practice to 10 minutes".
Step by step:
- Give grade, subject and class length.
- Paste objective and success criteria.
- Say what students know and what materials you have.
- List the sections and timings you want.
- Ask for a table, then improve with follow-ups.
Words to know:
- Mini-lesson: a short, focused teaching segment.
- Check for understanding: a quick way to see if students are following, like thumbs up or a whiteboard answer.
Try it now: Use the prompt pattern to get a full lesson draft for your objective from Lesson 1. Ask at least two follow-ups to improve it.
You can now get a usable, structured lesson draft from AI and improve it with follow-ups.

check.q: How should you treat an AI lesson draft?
options: As a draft from a fast but new colleague
As a finished plan ready to teach
As a plan approved by your district
As something to hide from colleagues
check.why: AI drafts are quick but need your judgment before use.

check.q: The AI lesson has no check for understanding. What would you do?
options: Teach it as it is
Start a new chat with a new tool
Remove the practice activities
Ask a follow-up: "Add a quick check for understanding after guided practice"
check.why: Follow-ups fill gaps in the draft without starting again.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Checking the plan: accuracy, alignment and bias
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Check an AI lesson plan with a five-point quality checklist.
This lesson builds toward: Given an AI lesson draft, you will check it with the five-point quality checklist and record your changes, fixing every problem found.
Every AI plan needs a teacher's check before it reaches students. Use five questions. Accurate: are all facts, examples, dates and answers correct? Aligned: does every activity move students toward the objective, and does the exit ticket measure it?
Right level: is it the right difficulty and length for these students and this time? Fair and inclusive: are examples, names and contexts respectful and varied, free of stereotypes, and accessible to students with disabilities and English learners? Doable: do you have the materials and time?
Mark what you changed. Over time this shows your team where AI plans tend to go wrong (often: too much content for the time, and activities that look busy but do not practice the objective).
Step by step:
- Accurate: check facts, examples and answers.
- Aligned: each activity serves the objective; exit ticket measures it.
- Right level for these students and this time.
- Fair and inclusive: no stereotypes; accessible.
- Doable with your materials; note what you changed.
Words to know:
- Alignment: when objectives, activities and assessment all match.
- Stereotype: an unfair, fixed idea about a group of people.
- Accessible: usable by every student, including those with disabilities.
Try it now: Run your lesson draft through the five-point check. Fix every problem and list the changes you made.
You can now check an AI lesson plan for accuracy, alignment, level, fairness and practicality.

check.q: What does alignment mean in a lesson plan?
options: The lesson is printed neatly
The lesson matches the textbook's order
Objectives, activities and assessment all match
The lesson uses the newest tools
check.why: Aligned lessons practice and assess the same thing the objective names.

check.q: The AI plan packs five activities into a 45-minute class. What would you change?
options: Cut it to fit the time, keeping the activities that practice the objective
Keep all five and rush
Add one more activity
Ask students to finish at home
check.why: Too much content for the time is the most common problem with AI plans.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Differentiation, units and team planning

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Building in differentiation
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Use AI to plan supports for students who need more help and challenge for those ready for more.
This lesson builds toward: Given a lesson and a class described by need, you will plan supports for three groups: needs more support, on level and ready for more, with IEP and 504 accommodations confirmed with a special education colleague.
Describe groups by need, never by name: "students who need more support with multi-step problems", "students on level", "students ready for more challenge". Ask AI for the same objective reached three ways: more scaffolding (worked examples, sentence starters, visuals), on-level practice, and extension (a harder problem or a transfer task).
Ask for supports that help everyone: clear visuals, vocabulary with pictures, choices in how students show learning. This approach, planning for variety from the start, is often called Universal Design for Learning (UDL); look up CAST's UDL Guidelines for more.
Students with IEPs or 504 plans must receive the accommodations in their plans; AI-generated supports never replace them. Check with the special education teacher, and do not put plan details into unapproved tools.
Step by step:
- Describe groups by need, not by name.
- Ask for three paths to the same objective.
- Ask for supports that help everyone: visuals, vocabulary, choice.
- Check IEP and 504 accommodations with the special education teacher.
- Keep plan details out of unapproved tools.
Words to know:
- Differentiation: adjusting teaching so students with different needs can reach the same goal.
- Scaffolding: temporary support, like worked examples or sentence starters.
- Universal Design for Learning (UDL): planning lessons for a wide range of learners from the start.
Try it now: Add differentiation to your lesson: ask AI for three paths to the objective, check them, and confirm which IEP or 504 accommodations still need to be planned with your special education colleague.
You can now plan support and challenge for different learners with AI while honoring required accommodations.

options: Giving advanced students extra work
Supports such as worked examples and sentence starters
Testing students before a lesson
Seating students in groups
check.why: Scaffolds help students reach the same goal with support.

check.q: AI suggests supports that differ from a student's IEP accommodation. What do you do?
options: Use the AI's supports instead
Ask the AI to decide
Drop both and teach as usual
Provide the IEP accommodation and plan with your special education colleague
check.why: IEP and 504 accommodations must still be provided, whatever AI suggests.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: From lesson to unit
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Draft a unit outline with AI and check its pacing.
This lesson builds toward: Given the unit your lesson belongs to, you will draft a unit outline with AI and adjust its pacing, adding a review day and three misconceptions to plan for.
A unit is a sequence of lessons toward bigger goals. Give AI the unit's standards (from your official source), the number of class days, holidays or testing days, and where students start. Ask for a day-by-day outline with objectives, key activities and checkpoints.
Check pacing first: AI often packs in too much. Make sure each lesson builds on the last, that there are review days and a plan for re-teaching, and that the end-of-unit assessment matches the objectives.
Use AI to brainstorm what it does well: a real-world project to anchor the unit, common misconceptions to plan for, and questions that make students think. You decide what fits.
Step by step:
- Give unit standards, number of days and calendar gaps.
- Ask for a day-by-day outline with objectives and checkpoints.
- Check pacing: cut, add review and re-teach days.
- Check that the final assessment matches the objectives.
- Use AI to brainstorm misconceptions and anchor projects.
Words to know:
- Unit: a set of lessons that work toward bigger learning goals.
- Pacing: how much is taught each day and how fast the class moves.
- Misconception: a common wrong idea students have about a topic.
Try it now: Ask AI for a ten-day outline of the unit your lesson belongs to. Adjust the pacing, add one review day, and list three misconceptions to plan for.
You can now draft and pace a unit outline with AI.

check.q: What should a unit outline prompt include?
options: Standards, number of days and calendar gaps
Students' names and grades
Only the unit title
The teacher's salary
check.why: Days and calendar gaps let AI propose realistic pacing.

check.q: The AI outline covers the unit in ten days with no review. What would you do?
options: Accept it as written
Add three more units
Adjust the pacing and add a review day
Remove the assessment
check.why: Pacing is the first thing to check, and review time is often missing.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Coaching teams to plan with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Turn your planning process into a template and coach a team to use it.
This lesson builds toward: For your team or PLC, you will turn your planning prompts and checklist into a team template and coach others to use it, tracking time saved and quality issues.
Leaders multiply good practice by making it repeatable. Turn what you learned into a planning template: the prompts for objective, full lesson, differentiation and unit, plus the five-point quality checklist.
Use it in a team or professional learning community (PLC) meeting: each teacher plans one lesson with the template, then partners swap plans and run the quality check on each other's. Discuss what AI got wrong; that builds shared judgment faster than any training slide.
Set expectations: AI-assisted plans are welcome, and teachers stay responsible for what they teach. Make sure only approved tools are used and no student information goes in. Ask teachers to note time saved and quality issues, so you know if the practice is working.
Step by step:
- Write the planning template: four prompts and the checklist.
- In a team meeting, each teacher plans one lesson with it.
- Partners swap and run the quality check.
- Discuss what AI got wrong.
- Set expectations and track time saved and quality issues.
Words to know:
- PLC: professional learning community: a team of teachers who meet to improve teaching together.
- Template: a reusable starting format.
Try it now: Final task: finish your complete lesson plan (objective, success criteria, hook, guided and independent practice, three groups, exit ticket with answers), check it with the five-point checklist, record your changes, and save your four prompts and the checklist as a team template.
You can now plan lessons with AI to a high standard and help a team do the same.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Objective and success criteria No objective, or the standard did not come from an official source. An objective and success criteria from a standard copied from the official source. The objective is written as a clear "I can" statement students understand. Complete lesson Missing the hook, guided or independent practice, or the exit ticket. Has a hook, guided and independent practice, and a three-question exit ticket with answers. Includes a check for understanding and fits the class length. Three groups Supports for one or more groups are missing. Supports for needs more support, on level and ready for more. Notes which IEP or 504 accommodations still need planning with a special education colleague. Quality checked Not checked, or changes not recorded. Checked with the five-point checklist, with each change and the reason recorded. The record shows patterns in where the AI plan went wrong. Team template Prompts not saved, or no checklist. Prompts and checklist saved as a template for the team. A colleague has used the template on their own lesson. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What should a team planning template include?
options: Only the final lesson
The prompts and the quality checklist
A list of banned tools
The AI tool's password
check.why: Prompts plus the checklist let others repeat the process and the checks.

check.q: You want to know if AI planning is helping your team. What do you track?
options: How many prompts each teacher writes
Which AI tool is newest
Nothing; ask once a year
Time saved and quality issues found
check.why: Time saved and quality issues show whether the process works.
